tasks.title: Multiple-Choice Guessing
tasks.context: A 10-question multiple-choice exam has 4 answer choices per question (1 correct). Person A guesses every answer at random (p = 0.25). Person B has studied and knows the material well (p = 0.90). To pass, a person needs at least 7 correct out of 10. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Person A's probability of scoring a perfect 10/10 by guessing is less than 0.01%.
The probability that Person B passes (scores at least 7 out of 10) equals the sum, from x = 7 to 10, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 10 and p = 0.90.
Person B is at least 300 times as likely as Person A to pass the exam.
Person B has a higher variance in number of correct answers than Person A.
Person A's mean (expected) number of correct answers is exactly one-fourth of the total number of questions.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — P(10/10) for Person A = $0.25^{10}$ ≈ 0.000095%, which is far below 0.01%.

Recall the perfect-run formula:

$$P(X=n)=p^{n}$$

Tip: Raising a probability below 0.5 to a power of 10 or more shrinks it dramatically — expect results in the fraction-of-a-percent range without needing a calculator.

TRUE — "At least 7 out of 10" is, by definition, the sum of the individual probabilities for 7, 8, 9, and 10 correct answers.

Key formula:

$$P(X=k)=\binom{n}{k}p^{k}(1-p)^{n-k}$$

Tip: Any 'at least k' phrase converts directly into a sum starting at k and ending at n — check the bounds match, not the underlying numbers.

FALSE — $P(X \ge 7)$ for B ≈ 98.72% and for A ≈ 0.35%. The ratio is about 282, which is less than 300 — close, but the statement's threshold is not met.

Key formula:

$$P(X=k)=\binom{n}{k}p^{k}(1-p)^{n-k}$$

Tip: Before accepting a big round-number ratio claim (like '300 times'), compute both $P(X \ge k)$ values and divide — don't round the ratio up in your head.

FALSE — Var(A) = 10 × 0.25 × 0.75 = 1.875. Var(B) = 10 × 0.90 × 0.10 = 0.90. Person A's variance is higher, not Person B's.

Key formula:

$$\mathrm{Var}(X)=np(1-p)$$

Tip: Variance = $np$·(1−p) is biggest when p is closest to 0.5. A p of 0.25 (guessing) is closer to 0.5 than 0.90 (expert), so the guesser's scores vary more — even though the expert scores higher on average.

TRUE — Mean(A) = n × p = 10 × 0.25 = 2.5, and one-fourth of 10 questions is also 2.5 — this always happens when p is exactly 1/4.

Key formula:

$$E[X]=np$$

Tip: When p is a simple fraction (like 1/4), the mean $np$ is just that same fraction of n — no multiplication needed, just simplify the fraction of the total.

tasks.title: Free Throws — Rookie vs All-Star
tasks.context: A basketball player takes 10 free throws. Player A is a rookie (p = 0.55 per shot). Player B is an all-star (p = 0.85 per shot). A "clutch" bonus is awarded for making at least 8 of the 10 shots. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Player B (the all-star) has more than a 20% chance of making all 10 shots in a row.
The probability that Player A earns the clutch bonus (at least 8 of 10 made) equals the sum, from x = 8 to 10, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 10 and p = 0.55.
Player B is more than 9 times as likely as Player A to earn the clutch bonus.
Player A's results have a larger standard deviation than Player B's.
The expected number of made shots for Player B is exactly 3 more than for Player A.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — P(10/10) for Player B = $0.85^{10}$ ≈ 19.69%, which is just under 20%.

Recall the perfect-run formula:

$$P(X=n)=p^{n}$$

Tip: For a 'perfect run' claim near a round-number threshold like 20%, compute p^n precisely rather than eyeballing — these are often deliberately close calls.

TRUE — "At least 8 of 10" is the sum of the individual probabilities for 8, 9, and 10 makes.

Key formula:

$$P(X=k)=\binom{n}{k}p^{k}(1-p)^{n-k}$$

Tip: Convert 'at least' straight into a sum from the threshold to n; the wording alone tells you the bounds.

FALSE — $P(X \ge 8)$ for B ≈ 82.02% and for A ≈ 9.96%. The ratio is about 8.24, which is more than 8 but not more than 9.

Tip: For ratio claims with a specific multiplier (like '9 times'), compute the exact ratio — don't round 8.24 up to 'about 9'.

TRUE — SD(A) = √(10 × 0.55 × 0.45) ≈ 1.573. SD(B) = √(10 × 0.85 × 0.15) ≈ 1.129. Player A's results are more spread out.

Key formula:

$$\mathrm{SD}(X)=\sqrt{np(1-p)}$$

Tip: Compare which p is closer to 0.5 to predict which person's results vary more, before computing exact numbers.

TRUE — Mean(B) −Mean(A) = (10 × 0.85) −(10 × 0.55) = 8.5 −5.5 = 3 exactly.

Key formula:

$$E[X]=np$$

Tip: When two means share the same n, their difference is just n × (difference in p) — here 10 × (0.85 − 0.55) = 3, no need to compute each mean separately.

On average, Inspector A does not meet the certification bar of 18 correctly classified items.

$$P(X=k)=\binom{n}{k}p^{k}(1-p)^{n-k}$$
